title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: Which statement best separates a workflow from an agent?

options.text: A workflow makes one model call; an agent makes several in a row
In a workflow, code fixes the steps; in an agent, the model picks them
A workflow cannot use any tools; an agent is the only design that can
A workflow has no model inside it; an agent is built around a model

items.stem: In your makerspace assistant, the Python code always calls search_manuals with the student's question, then makes one model call that writes an answer from the top three passages, then returns it. Nothing else can happen. What is this design?

options.text: An agent, because it calls a tool and then calls a language model
An agent, because the model chooses the wording of the final answer
A workflow, because the code decides every step and its order
A workflow, because it makes fewer than five calls to the model

items.stem: Assume every model call costs 2 cents, and tool runs cost nothing. A fixed workflow answers a booking request with exactly 2 model calls. An agent handles the same request with one model call per step: one call for each of its 4 tool requests, plus one call for the final answer. How many cents more does the agent cost per request than the workflow?
Which part of the makerspace assistant is the best candidate for a fixed workflow rather than an agent?

options.text: Working out why a student's 3D print keeps failing halfway through
Answering open questions that may need several manuals and the calendar
Helping a student plan which machines a new project will need
Booking a slot once machine, date and time are known: check, book, confirm

items.stem: Your sponsor gave you a small model budget. In one sentence, give one reason a fixed workflow is a good fit for a task whose steps are the same every time.
In one sentence, what is the main thing you give up by choosing a fixed workflow instead of an agent for a task?
